dedupe_keys.name: houston food bank locating food distribution points after a hurricane harvey like disaster

description: This case study builds a location-allocation model that decides which food pantries in a food bank network should act as points of distribution (PODs) after a disaster, and which demand zones each should serve. The authors, researchers at Pennsylvania State University, the University at Buffalo and the University of Missouri–St. Louis, published it in an open-access journal article. The model minimises total social cost, the sum of delivery costs and the suffering of survivors expressed through an empirically estimated deprivation cost function for food and water, which grows non-linearly with the time a survivor waits, including travel to the POD and queuing there. It was tested on the Houston Food Bank network in instances that mimic a response to a future disaster like Hurricane Harvey in 2017, and also examines delivery frequency and shipment size. The article is free to read under a Creative Commons Attribution licence. Caveats: the instances are hypothetical designs, not an evaluated real response, and the deprivation cost function is borrowed from earlier empirical work. The study found that choosing POD locations by social cost changes which pantries open and how often they are resupplied, giving practical guidance for prioritising survivors' needs. Simulation uses: an optimisation template for post-disaster food distribution and emergency supply planning. Related records: the Harris County food pantry access study (case_study-harris-county-food-pantry-access-after-flooding) looks at pantry access after flooding in the same area.
